Sample text:
---
I'll write about the particular quality of light in late afternoon, and how it seems to hold memory.

---

There is a hour, somewhere between four and six, when the world tilts toward gold. Not the harsh gold of noon, which bleaches and flattens, but something softer, more forgiving. The light comes in low, at an angle that makes everything cast a shadow, even the shadows themselves seem to lean. I have noticed that people photograph this light obsessively—golden hour, they call it, as if naming it could capture it. But it escapes. It always escapes.

I think about my grandmother's kitchen, how the afternoon light would come through the window above the sink and land on the linoleum in a perfect rectangle. She kept a geranium in a red pot on the sill, and the light would pass through the leaves and project their shapes onto the floor, trembling slightly whenever the wind moved. I used to lie on that floor with my back against the cabinets, watching the green shadows breathe. I didn't know then that I was practicing for grief. That I was learning how to hold something beautiful that would not stay.

The physicists say light is both wave and particle, that it behaves differently depending on how you look at it. This seems like a metaphor for almost everything. The same afternoon can be peaceful or lonely, depending on who is watching, what they have lost, what they are waiting for. I have stood in identical rooms at identical times and felt completely different things. The light does not change. Only I do.

There is a photograph I keep meaning to take but never do. It's of the empty lot behind my apartment building, where a house burned down three years ago. The lot is overgrown now, full of milkweed and something that looks like wild carrot. In the late afternoon, the light comes through the gap where the house used to be and illuminates the weeds so completely that they seem to glow from within. It is the most beautiful thing I see most days. I don't take the photograph because I am afraid it will look ordinary in the frame, a picture of weeds. But also because some things feel like they belong to the moment, to the particular angle of my head, to the temperature of the air, to whatever is happening in my body that I cannot name. The camera would fix it, make it permanent, and I am not sure I want that. I am not sure I want anything permanent.

My father used to say that light travels at a constant speed, that nothing can go faster, that this is the fundamental structure of the universe. He was an engineer, practical, suspicious of poetry. But he said this with something like reverence, as if he were describing a law of nature that also applied to the heart. I think about this when I am far from him, when the light in my apartment is different from the light in his house, when I realize that the photons hitting my skin left the sun eight minutes ago, that I am always seeing the past, always slightly behind the present. The light that warms me now was already old when it began its journey. Everything I see is a memory. Everything I feel is a memory. The present is a fiction we tell ourselves to keep moving.

I have started walking in the evenings, not for exercise, though my body needs it, but for the light. There is a path along the river that faces west, and if I time it right, I can walk directly into the sunset. It is disorienting, walking toward the source of light rather than away from it. My eyes water. I squint. I feel foolish and holy at the same time. People pass me going the other direction, already in shadow, already moving toward evening, toward dinner, toward whatever comes next. I keep walking toward the fire.

The river is brown most of the year, silt-heavy, carrying everything the land gives it. But in the late afternoon, the surface becomes a mirror, imperfect, broken by current, but still reflecting the sky, the trees, the particular orange and pink and violet that the day is dissolving into. I have seen herons standing in the shallows, motionless, waiting. I have seen the same heron, I think, on three different evenings, though I cannot be sure. They all look the same to me, patient, prehistoric, belonging to a time before urgency. I want to be like that. I want to stand in the water and wait for whatever comes, without wanting it to come faster or slower, without wanting it at all, simply being present for it.

There is a man who fishes from the bank, always in the same spot, always wearing a hat with a brim so wide it seems to belong to another century. I have never spoken to him. I don't know his name. But I have started to recognize his silhouette against the light, the particular angle of his shoulders, the way he holds the rod as if in conversation with something invisible. Last week, I saw him catch a fish—something small, silver, struggling—and he held it above the water for a moment, just a moment, before releasing it. I don't know if he was admiring it or apologizing. The light was too bright to see his face. I walked past without stopping, not wanting to break whatever was happening between him and the river, between him and the fish, between him and the evening.

I think about all the evenings I have wasted. Not wasted in the sense of doing nothing, but wasted in the sense of not paying attention. The evenings spent scrolling, consuming, filling time with noise so that I would not have to hear the silence. The evenings spent worrying about tomorrow, already living in a future that has not arrived. The evenings spent with people who did not see me, or with myself in ways that felt like performance rather than presence. I am trying to do better. I am trying to let the light in, literally and otherwise, to stand in it without trying to capture it, to let it change me without demanding that it stay.

The light is changing now, as I write this. The room is dimming. I can see my hands on the keyboard, but the details are softening, becoming impression rather than information. Soon I will need to turn on a lamp, and the lamp will be wrong, too yellow, too contained, nothing like the vast, indifferent generosity of the sun. But I will turn it on anyway, because I want to keep writing, keep reaching for words, keep trying to say something true about this day that is ending, this life that is continuing, this strange and beautiful difficulty of being here, in this body, at this time, with this particular quality of light that will not last, that never lasts, that is always already leaving.
---
